utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will ask for certain associated exhibits to be admitted. I intend to use some with him, and, so I understand it, the process is to tender them as I go and ultimately decide them at the end of the testimony. If that's all right. I have a brief summary of the testimony I would like to read into the record at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time of his testimony in the Popovic et al case, Dr. Parsons was the director of the forensic sciences for the International Commission for Missing Persons which operates a highly experienced DNA laboratory system active since 2001. In October 2007, the organisation received an ISO 17025 accreditation, a significant international standard for forensic DNA analysis. The ICMP mandate is the identification of missing persons. Its task is principally threefold. 1, to assist governments with the issue of missing persons; 2, to conduct a civil society initiative; and 3, to provide forensic assistance by providing DNA identifications. Although relevant in part to the Tribunal's proceedings, the ICMP's work is conducted wholly independently. Dr. Parsons's responsibilities included supervising three forensic science divisions, the examinations and excavation division, the DNA laboratory system, the DNA identification and co-ordination division. Dr. Parsons explained the nature and the reliability of DNA testing generally, as well as the specific processes involving nuclear STR typing, a well-established technology validated and accepted in the scientific community as the standard in forensic diagnosis. He further noted that as part of its accreditation, the ICMP is subject to a formal review process and technical audits. Many Standard Operating Procedures, SOPs, document the DNA testing processes carried out by the ICMP. These SOPs shared with other laboratories reflect fundamental science and widely used procedures. Many are referenced in Dr. Parsons's methodology report which covers the period from 2001 to 2008. Dr. Parsons testified that the International Commission on Missing Persons DNA matching procedure is robust, documented and regulated. Match reports express the DNA tests and require a minimum threshold of statistical surety of 99.95 per cent to be issued. Where there is presumptive evidence of identity, such as in the presence of artefacts, that threshold is 99 per cent statistical surety. The ICMP has in place a formal system of review for all DNA reports. As of Dr. Parsons's 2009 testimony, the ICMP's data reflected 6023 individual victims connected to the Srebrenica events. Mr. President, that concludes my summary and I do have some questions to put to Dr. Parsons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll come back to that in just a moment. Let me clarify first. This was created after the methodology report that was the subject of your Popovic testimony covering the period from 2001 to 2008; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That's correct. This was intended as an update to that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let me just show you 65 ter 23672. I understand that we have some problems with that one. But can you explain a little bit about the nature of the protocols that have changed since the 2001 through 2008 methodology report. Are these substantive changes to the techniques, for example, that are employed by the organisation?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I'd like to emphasise that they do not reflect any substantial overarching change to the basic technology that is utilised in the laboratory. We continue to use nuclear STR typing as our predominant form of identification. The predominant changes reflected in this document, if I remember it correctly, would relate to a new and improved extraction method for isolating DNA from degraded skeletal remains. We continue to perform research at the ICMP to improve methodologies and we then tested and validated a new and more sensitive method for recovery of DNA. There is also some instrumentation update aspects to this where we would replace older models of instrumentation with new state-of-the-art models of instrumentation and associated changes associated with that. But really rather routine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are these kinds of protocol changes connected to any changes in the platforms, for example, the nature of the types of tests that you run?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Not fundamentally to the nature of the types of tests that we run. You use the word "platform," and in many instances "platform" is a word that is applied to instrumentation, so I would say that maybe our platforms have changed. That is to say, the model of instrument that we run the profiles on is new.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Dr. Parsons, have your responsibilities as director of forensic sciences at the ICMP changed in any way since your testimony here in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No, they have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you just briefly remind us of what specific entities or what your responsibilities are with respect to different divisions and sections within the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: In general, my role is to direct the scientific standards of the laboratory and to be responsible for the implementation of our scientific quality management system that oversees the manner in which scientific results are produced. With regard to supervision of divisions within the ICMP, I would refer to the nice summary that you gave just a little bit ago. There are three main divisions. One is the DNA laboratory division where samples, either blood samples or prepared small bone samples, are tested for nuclear DNA profiles and a DNA profile is obtained. A second division that I oversee is the identification co-ordination division and this is the central facility at the ICMP where samples are received either from mortuary facilities by a forensic pathologist or an anthropologist or blood samples that have been donated by family members who are seeking their missing persons. And those samples enter the identification co-ordination division and are then accessioned to the ICMP system in a manner that strips them of all information that would potentially bias subsequent steps. So they are given a random number, which we refer to as a bar code, and then those are sent to the DNA laboratory system in a blind manner to allow an objective testing process. The identification co-ordination system then plays -- division, identification co-ordination division then plays an important role at the other end of the process. After DNA profiles are obtained in the laboratory, those profiles are sent to the identification co-ordination division where matching, genetic matching is performed. Databases of family reference DNA profiles are searched for each and every profile that we get from a human remains bone sample, and in that way, DNA matches are identified. And it is the identification co-ordination division that issues those match reports. The third division that I'm responsible for in terms of overall oversight is what was referred to as the excavations and exhumations -- examinations division, excavations and examinations division. We've actually since changed the name. The function remains the same. We now refer to it as the archeology and anthropology division. And those are the people that provide technical assistance in the excavation of graves, the recovery of human remains, as well as the anthropological examination in a mortuary setting after those remains are recovered to assess a biological profile to determine whether the remains represent a single individual or possibly have been co-mingled to represent multiple individuals, and importantly, also in many instances provide technical assistance in sampling those remains for DNA testing that are then sent to the laboratory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My respect for the interpreters. Now you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the current accreditation status is of the DNA laboratory system of the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Both the DNA laboratory system and the identification co-ordination division are accredited to the International ISO 17025 standard through the German national accreditation agency DACH. That's the abbreviation for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And has there been any change in the protocols or procedures employed by the organisation since it was accredited and since you've testified in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: You ask specifically about protocols, and as an accredited laboratory we operate strictly off of a set of procedures which are referred to as Standard Operating Procedures and those define the conduct of each of the scientists involved in the process of the DNA lab, in the matching. And in fact, those protocols are routinely updated to reflect changes and or improvements in methodology or to accommodate, for example, a new instrumentation that requires different steps for the entry of information. These kind of things. So there have been many changes with regard to our large battery of Standard Operating Procedures. But, again, I would emphasise nothing fundamental has changed with regard to our accreditation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do any of the changes that have occurred with respect to the procedures or protocols employed by the organisation reflect on the standard or the accuracy of testing procedures that took place prior to the implementation of those protocols and procedures?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The fact that we may proactively implement steps that we consider to decrease the chance for human error, for example, or to increase the sensitivity of a DNA extraction, those kind of things, we have no reason to believe that they impugn the accuracy of previously reported results.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Has the ICMP carried out, for lack of a better term, spot-checks, for example, of analyses that have been conducted prior to the implementation of new instruments or new procedures to determine the accuracy of the previously analysed results?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes. In a number of ways. One way is from -- is through blind proficiency testing in the laboratory, where the identification co-ordination division in an anonymous and blind manner submits to the DNA laboratory samples that the DNA laboratory has previously reported a result on. Now the laboratory receives a new sample, doesn't know that it has been previously tested, and then produces a result again. And then, of course, within the quality management system we would check to make sure that they got a consistent result, and this is a -- it's known as an internal blind proficiency test of the laboratory. We also routinely review data generated in previous years when it relates to new matches that are being made. So we will have the situation where reference DNA profiles may have been generated in 2004, but we have now, in 2011, say, received a bone sample that's given a profile that matches those reference samples from 2004. Under those circumstances we will then perform a new technical review of the family reference samples that were generated previously to ensure that they are up to present-day standards. If there is any question with regard to the final review process on the DNA match report, we do not hesitate to retest those samples to confirm.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In the instances where you had an occasion to go back and test reference samples or other samples that were obtained prior to the implementation of a new procedure or protocol, have you achieved results that are consistent with the previously obtained results or inconsistent with the previously obtained results?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Almost universally the results are consistent. Well, if I may return to your previous question and add one more instance regarding analysis of previous data and that relates to -- I mentioned earlier that we now have improved protocols for extraction of DNA from degraded skeletal remains. And we went back to all DNA profiles from human remains samples that were generated from 2001 to 2004, the earlier days of the ICMP, and these are profiles that have not matched to family references. So we're concerned why they may not have been matching. The most -- the most typical reason is that we simply don't have reference samples for them to match, but we wondered if improved protocols and a reanalysis of that data could make it possible for us to discern additional matches within those early profiles. So we went through an exercise of investigating 1.582 unmatched profiles from bones that had been generated between 2001 and 2004. And through an extremely labourious process of technical review, we found -- I believe it was a single instance where they -- the previous profile was incorrect, according to our analysis, and we found 16 instances where improved data allowed a DNA match to be found when it previously couldn't be found. So basically we added more genetic data to those cases and were able to make a match.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation, Dr. Parsons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And then if we look a little bit -- if we can go to the right, please, of this document. We can see the name of a pathologist and we can see the jurisdiction BiH/MPI. Can you tell us what that reflects?
