utterances.text: The samples that we receive are under the authority of a court-appointed forensic pathologist - in this case, the individual named here - and the overarching authority that -- that allows him to conduct these analyses in this instance is the Missing Persons Institute, a national agency in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us whether or not the information that's contained in this particular document is coded or uncoded?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: At the upper part of this match report are listed a number of DNA profiles and that would be the genetic information that was obtained from the samples in question. This is an instance where the genetic data is coded in a way that does not -- that protects the privacy of the individual. So in viewing this match report, anyone who has it is not able to know the true genetic profile of the individuals involved, although they are able to discern what date was obtained and also discern patterns of relationships between the related individuals that are represented on this match report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And could you tell us in plain English what the conclusion expresses here with regard to the possible identification of the individual in this report?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, before he does that, I would like to inquire why this document could not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not concerned with the identification of some family members of victims? But probably we will be assisted by hearing from you, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, there are two issues. One is that it relates to the identification of the family members. And the second issue is because it essentially identifies the remains, the person who was recovered from the exhumation, and at this point it is unclear whether or not those family members have been notified that that person has been so identified and the case closed. So that's the reason why I've asked to proceed in this manner and not to broadcast it although we are talking about it at least publicly. And that's why I hesitate to use the names of any of the individuals named in this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is to be admitted, your submission is that it should be admitted under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it to be admitted, do we have to admit it under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. First of all, I notice the document is from 2009, so I find it very surprising if the family wouldn't have been notified by now that the remains of the deceased had been located. But apart from that issue, I don't understand why the identity of relatives is something that is -- something should be protected and people don't have protective measures in the normal situation in a domestic court. When you have a homicide, there's no hiding from the public or making under seal the identity of relatives of the victim. It is all part of a public trial. And so absent any sensitive issues that could cause someone grief such as learning through these proceedings of the identity of the bones of a loved one, I don't see why, in principle, why we should keep from the public this material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it is your argument, isn't it, that DNA information can be revealed to public? Of anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, he's -- I think he has testified that this document doesn't reveal the actual DNA of these people themselves. So given -- that's -- when I heard that testimony, that's what prompted me to think that there was really no reason why this document could not be made public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And I appreciate the arguments that Mr. Robinson has made but I think he himself has acknowledged and identified the very issue, or the crux of the issue here, which is to the extent that it is not known whether or not the family members of the person identified in this document have been notified, this is the very reason why this information shouldn't be broadcast. Despite the fact that Mr. Robinson may find it difficult to believe that that hasn't happened yet. In certain circumstances these individuals are far-flung and it's not clear what contact they have with respect to information about their loved ones, whether they can be located, and so there's a -- and there is an -- I'm sure Mr. Robinson is aware, as Dr. Stojkovic is, that there ask a formal process by which those notifications take place which involve pathologists, they involve court order, et cetera, which is something that is a little bit away or outside of the ICMP's direct remit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: But, Mr. President, couldn't the Prosecution and the ICMP identify for us those what I would hope to be very rare situations where they've had for three years the identity of a victim and not notified the family members and otherwise be able to use in public the remaining documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we leave it at that and proceed dealing -- dealing with these items sort of confidentially and sort it out later on. But probably you can deal with Dr. Parsons during your further -- remaining examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think I can. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think I was asking you about trying to express in plain English, if you will, the conclusion that is expressed in this report.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The conclusion statement communicates the strength of the DNA evidence that favours the association of this set of human remains to the family members as listed on this report. The first number that we quote where it says the DNA results obtained from the bone sample - I won't read the number - are 42.6 e 12 times more likely if the bone sample originated from an individual related to the blood references in a manner as described on this report. What that means is - in getting back to the plain English part of it - first I will -- I will indicate that the 42.6 e 12 is a shorthand notation for exponential in base 10. So that number reflects 42.6, followed by 12 zeros. So that would be 42.6, if I have this right, trillion times - is that right? I think that's right - more likely. And that is the number by which we are more sure of this potential association after having done the test. So there may be some prior reason to suspect that this bone sample belongs to this individual. Having done the DNA test, we are now 42.6 trillion times more sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you briefly explain to the Chamber what is meant by prior odds of 1 over 4500 as we see here.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Right. That number, the -- the -- prior odds is the level of certainty which we are updating. So that is ICMP's estimate, in this case, of how sure we were before we did the DNA test. And the convention that the ICMP uses is simply to consider the number of missing persons understood to be missing from a particular region or event. In this case, I -- I don't -- I can't recall where precisely this comes from, but it would have been an event where we consider that there were 4.500 people missing generally. And so our prior odds were simply that there is one chance in 4.500 that this bone sample would be from this particular individual prior to doing the DNA test, so a pretty low chance because there were so many people missing. In considering only that number of missing people, we then did the DNA test and are 42 trillion times more sure, and then when we combine that with the prior odds or the prior probability of 1 in 4.500, we get a final posterior probability of relatedness and that is the number that the 99.99999 per cent value. And that basically -- that is the number that corresponds to really how sure we are in the end that this would be the individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would offer this exhibit into evidence. Under seal. It does contain other such match reports but I don't think it is necessary to show the witness each of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As a sample, the sample page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would like to actually tender the entire document because it concerns 58 individuals, the identities of whom have been established in relation to an event that is charged in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're going to tender it separately or tender it all together?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's all one document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we deal with it at the end --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're not going to deal with the remainder of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm not planning to deal with the remainder of the document. They're all match reports concerning the one event that is indicated on this particular page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I don't think it is really necessary for them to go through each of the 58, so it's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 22858 shall be assigned Exhibit P4639, under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And given the time, if it is convenient, we'll have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll break for an hour and resume at 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.31 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours, good afternoon. If I could have in e-court shown to the witness, please, 65 ter 22860.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Dr. Parsons, what I'm showing you -- first of all, do you recognise what this document is?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In this particular instance, we can see a case number KOR031003-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And, again, this concerns the Koricanske Stijene, which, as I mentioned, for Your Honours' benefit, is referred to the indictment, Scheduled Incident B 15.6.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how would you describe -- or, rather, what is this document, Dr. Parsons?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: This is also a DNA match report generated by the ICMP. It looks different than the version that you showed before the break. It is simply an older format was that was in use at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could just go down to the bottom of the page for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Here we see the date, 24 November 2004. Is that consistent with the format that this particular report is in?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I would be -- I would have no reason to consider it inconsistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Parsons.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender this exhibit as well. This one concerns four individuals related to the same incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I don't know if this is being offered to be tendered under seal, but I just happened to notice that in the Mrdja indictment it lists all the victims of Koricanske Stijene, including the one whose profile was admitted under seal before the break. So I think that the possibility of announcing someone's remains have been found when it wasn't already known that they were victims of this incident is non-existent, so these should not be admitted under seal but admitted for public consumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, and perhaps my colleague is under a misimpression. There are a couple of issues that attend to this question. One is the privacy interests of the individuals whose blood samples have been analysed. And then there are the interests of obviously the victim that has been identified. And then there are also privacy interests as regards the relationship between those individuals who have submitted blood samples, between -- among those individuals, I should say, and the victim. So it is not clear to me that even if a notification has occurred or even if it is known, the identity of a victim, that it is necessarily known among the donors who gave blood to identify that victim what the status among them is, and so I don't know that Mr. Robinson's arguments actually obtain, notwithstanding the fact that the identity of the victim is known.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, again, Mr. President, I think that in domestic proceedings these matters are all public and it's only -- and even in this Tribunal something is not supposed to be in closed session unless it is in the interests of justice and it is presumed that all of our proceedings are to be open. And I don't think that a fact that the an individual is related to another individual who has died implicates a privacy interest such that we should close the proceedings and make that information not available to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it that -- it was my understanding that, Mr. Vanderpuye, you would deal with that issue with Dr. Parsons in -- in your -- in the course of your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm happy to do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Dr. Parsons, if you're able, can you articulate, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber and for the Defence, the reasons why there may be privacy interests with respect to the publication of these reports?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The principle reason is the one that you proffered a little while ago, relating to our knowledge of family notification. It does not seem appropriate to the ICMP to have the potential that a family member will learn of the fate of their loved one through viewing public court proceedings here. Moreover, with reference to several instances where domestic court proceedings have been referred to, I would suggest that this is a slightly different context with regard to perception on the part of victims and victims' family, with regard to their own personal security. And from that standpoint, it would seem that there's a privacy issue with regard to having participated in a process that would identify their loved one, and, moreover, potentially be entered into a criminal proceedings such as this one here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is it possible that the information that's contained in a report such as this may reveal a familial relationship or the lack thereof between donors for the purposes of identifying a particular victim?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: In the instance where even coded genetic data is listed on the DNA match report, there is a potential for genetic relationships to be revealed, and we would consider that to be private information to that family.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Parsons.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if there are additional questions, clarifying questions you'd like me to ask, I'll be happy to pose them as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, given the information given by Dr. Parsons and following the practice of other Chambers, we'll admit it under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4640, under seal, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I can please show the witness 65 ter 22859 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is a document, Dr. Parsons, that concerns 38 individuals identified in relation to the incident of which I previously spoke concerning the Koricani cliffs. First, can you tell us what we're looking at here?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: This is yet another type of DNA match report that is issued by the ICMP. However, this particular document would be an internal DNA match report that we use for purposes of final review. Blacked out in the lower left of this document are a series of signature lines that would represent the responsible scientists who are involved in the final review process and the genetic data that is present on this report that here has appropriately been blacked out would -- would represent the genuine and authentic data that we consider to be private data.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Here we have another report similar to the one that we saw in the previous exhibit. Is this also consistent with the style or the format of the report that you referred to previously as an earlier iteration?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would similarly tender this document under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4641, under seal, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness, and I believe this also should not be broadcast, 65 ter 23660. I think this has to be displayed in Sanction, so I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Dr. Parsons, do you recognise what we have on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I do not. It says "E-court surrogate sheet," does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Ah, okay. We'll have to adjust that for you, I think. Do you have the exhibit in front of you now, Dr. Parsons?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And what is it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: This is a list of DNA match reports that have been issued by the ICMP from the period of November 2001 to August 2011, representing DNA match reports considered by the ICMP to be related to the fall of Srebrenica in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And we can see that it's split up into several different tabs. One relating to Srebrenica event, Zepa event, and then there's a tab for cases inconclusively associated and cases excluded. What I'd like to do is to just go briefly into the Srebrenica event list, for you to indicate to the Trial Chamber what's in there, what the various designations are. So if we can just go into that page. I think we have it right on the first, and we can see obviously some names, date of birth, and then protocol ID. Can you tell us what that means briefly?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The protocol ID is an internal number assigned by the ICMP that simply relates to the DNA match report itself. So we can consider it the number associated with the DNA match report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is it unique to a particular sample match or to an individual?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: It is unique to that sample match, to that match report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Next to that we see case ID. Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That is the designation that came with the sample to the ICMP as an identifier of that sample.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As we move a bit -- and that is unique to the sample, let me just ask before we move on to the next column?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could move to the right side a little, we can see ICMP ID. Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That is a number also internally assigned by the ICMP, but in this case, it refers to the reported missing person. So it's specific to that individual that was reported to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I think we can see an example of that in rows 7 and 8, where we have the same individual named with a common ICMP ID and then we have a site name next to that. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we go over to the right of the screen a little bit more, I'd like -- a little bit more. I'd like to ask you explain a couple of things here. We see jurisdiction. What does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That is the agency under whose authority that grave-site where the sample came from was excavated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can we go a little bit more to the right. A couple more columns.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Here we have the place of disappearance and the protocol ID. The place of disappearance here we have on this particular frame alternates -- well, not alternates, but contains Potocari and forest. Can you explain what that means?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: These are the designations that the ICMP has listed as a result of interacting with the families who reported these individuals missing as to their last reported -- as to their place of disappearance. In association with the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995, there were two major events involving victims. A large column of men in the days preceding July 10th and 11th, trying to escape over land from Srebrenica toward Tuzla, and those individuals that were involved in that -- in that action would be listed as missing from, quote/unquote, forest. And then there was another set of men and boys, almost exclusively but not entirely exclusively, that remained in Potocari at the DutchBat facility and other environs and that were subsequently disappeared -- subsequently became missing and were reported by the family members to have remained in Potocari at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Generally where does this information come from for the purposes of this list, for ICMP purposes?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: It comes from the detailed interactions that we have with family members at the time that we take the information that is needed from them to register a missing person and to obtain related types of information that we would capture.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Protocol ID. Can you tell us what that means?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Again, that's the -- that's the protocol number that is associated with the DNA match report and -- and there are basically two kinds of protocol numbers. One is a main number which is -- if we look at the top of list -- this list, 9662-07, that would be a main case. If we drop down a little bit, we can see a protocol number with an R as a suffix and that would be -- that would indicate a sample that has been reassociated to a previously identified sample from that same individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And we can see on the far right column the designations of main cases and reassociations. Is that what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to go over to the cases inconclusively associated, and here we have very similar entries. Can you, first of all, explain very briefly what this designation is, inconclusively associated cases?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, this is a small number of DNA match reports which based on the information we have may very well be associated with the Srebrenica event. But there's a possibility that they are not. So we have separated them out into -- into a separate sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the possibilities -- the limited possibility that they may be associated with the Srebrenica event in this -- in this particular instance shows up in what types of examples, can you give us?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not in a position to recall the details of all these cases, but I'll give you a simple example of the kind of thing that would put someone on this list. And that would be in the instance where we have related missing persons. So let's say we have two brothers that are both reported to us as missing, and one of these brothers is reported missing as associated with Srebrenica and the other from some event separate from Srebrenica, maybe happened several years before the 1995 event. Now, if we only have, for example, parents as family reference samples for these two siblings, then the DNA information we get actually does not allow us to distinguish which sibling is which. If we get a DNA match from just one of them, we don't know which one it is. Now if we had children as references from that individual, then we would be able to tell; but if we have only parents, the only thing we would know is that this individual is an offspring of these parents and we wouldn't know which is which. So here we will have someone that has been identified as either the one brother or the other brother possibly therefore associated with Srebrenica, or possibly not, depending on which of the two siblings it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us -- if we can go to the right side of this, rather, we can see that this particular spreadsheet contains information or explanations, rather, concerning the disposition of some of these inconclusively associated cases, yes?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to go now to the cases excluded tab and again we can go all the way to the right of the screen since it is substantially similar in form. And we have some explanations as to this designation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In these circumstances, first, can you tell us what excluded cases comprise?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: All right. In order to be listed as one of these 11 cases that have been listed as excluded from Srebrenica they would have had to previously been on one of the other two lists. They would have had to either previously been on the list of Srebrenica cases or on the list of inconclusively associated with Srebrenica. So an example here of how someone could arrive on this list, we would imagine the exact scenario that I mentioned before with two siblings, one reported missing from Srebrenica, the other reported not from Srebrenica. And if an identification has been concluded on one of the siblings from a Srebrenica -- a known Srebrenica-related grave, we then can infer, having identified the other one as well, that he is not associated with the Srebrenica and therefore he has been migrated into this category. Now I'll mention also that the list that we put together for Srebrenica associated is based in one primary instance on the information that we get from families, but there's a great deal of additional cross-checking that goes into our process. And moreover, we have generated and produced a number of versions of these lists over the years and presented them to Defence and to the Prosecution and the Court. In the course of doing so, we did identify a very small number of cases that were previously on the Srebrenica list that -- that we felt should not be added. Having gone through this list now multiple times over years, we've not found any additional ones that we feel it were mis-categorised and we have this set of 11 now, that -- that were previously on one of the two lists that we feel should not be on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We don't have any objection to the exhibit being admitted, but returning once again to the issue of -- of the public nature of this, I understand this is to be admitted under seal. But I'm wondering if we can admit at least some of the information on this chart publicly. And the reason for that is that we have now the submission by the ICMP that there are all these people who have died during the Srebrenica events. What if -- and they don't -- if these names are not public, what if there is somebody sitting in Salt Lake City, Utah, whose name is on this list and says, Wait a minute, there's a mistake here, I didn't die. Or what if there's a family member who sees the name of somebody who they know died in 1992, or somebody who was with somebody in the fights in the forest in Srebrenica who knows that the person was not a victim of an execution, these people can come forward if the list of victims is public and we can know exactly, this is a way of testing publicly the evidence that the ICMP stands behind. But if this is under seal, then we're deprived of that opportunity. So I understand why DNA coding and perhaps some family relationships might be otherwise under seal, but the names of the victims, in our view, ought to be part of the public record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm quite certain that there is a Srebrenica list of missing and dead individuals associated with Srebrenica that is part of the 94 bis record at least in these proceedings, perhaps associated with the testimony of Dr. Tabeau or Dr. Brunborg, and I think Mr. Robinson perhaps would be aware of that. So I don't know that it's necessary for this particular list to be tendered publicly insofar as the information that Mr. Robinson is seeking concerning the victims of the Srebrenica events is accessible to him, and it is in fact, as I understand it, available publicly in other proceedings as well. Perhaps I can be -- perhaps Mr. Robinson can correct me, but in terms of the list of victims being public, there's no problem with that. The problem is the DNA identification of those victims and that's another -- that's a completely different issue. To the extent that this list can be redacted, there's no problem, as I understand it, with making available publicly the names of each and every one of the victims that are on this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think if we could arrive at some kind of public redacted version of this document, that would be a good solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is your submission limited to this exhibit or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, no, my submission is actually for all of the exhibits that are going under seal. To the extent that the information can be publicly available without compromising the interests that the Trial Chamber has identified, we would like that to be the case. Because we think this is part of the scrutiny of the ICMP's work that is important. So to the extent that their work can be in the sunshine, as it were, we are in favour of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I hear from you, Mr. Vanderpuye, again, with respect to all the other ICMP reports that we have so far admitted under seal. In relation to producing a public redacted version.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, with -- in respect of all of the other documents that we have under seal, the problem with producing a public redacted version of those documents would entail essentially removing all the familial relations that underlie the particular identifications. I don't know if it is possible to just list them on the spreadsheet and that might be perhaps the most effective way to do it. And these are of the victims but not necessarily of the donors and the family members that led to the identification of those victims. But fundamentally the problem is this, is that by associating those names or the particular names with the ICMP, we are in fact revealing that they have been identified by DNA analysis which, of course, presents the same issue as concerns the identification of these individuals by the ICMP in relation to the events at Srebrenica or wherever the case may be. So the problem is fundamentally the same, and that is that the notification of the family members hasn't been established so that they're not finding out for the first time that their loved one is showing up in multiple graves spread out all over Eastern Bosnia for the first time through these proceedings. That's the crux of the issue and that is not really mitigated in any way by the redactions. But I'm sure that some solution can be worked out with the Defence that would satisfy them and also protect the interests of those relatives who have yet to be notified. I reiterate that the fact that one relative may have been notified does not mean that every other relative who has contributed blood to identify a victim has been so notified, and that's really what we're trying to protect against, the harm to those people from discovering the fate of their loved ones in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The Prosecution started off this presentation by saying that the information was -- identity of the victims was already publicly available in the reports of Brunborg and others, so I don't understand. If the identity of the victims is already publicly available, why is there a problem now with not making that information available here?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Robinson knows that there is a combination of individuals who are missing. There are a combination of individuals who have been identified forensically by pathology reports and other artefact evidence. And there are those individuals who have been identified by DNA analysis. What we're talking about here, strictly speaking, are those individuals who have been identified through the DNA process as opposed to having been identified by some other means as a victim of these crimes. That is essentially the issue. If somebody is on the ICRC list as missing, they're missing. If they they've been identified through a DNA process, they're dead. And there's a big difference between those two positions as concerns individuals who have not been notified as to the fate of their loved ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, our position we would like the -- the list of people who the ICMP has identified through DNA evidence as deceased from the Srebrenica events to be public, and if there is some problem of notification, perhaps we can give the ICMP 30 days, or whatever, to notify those people before it is made public. But otherwise, they're shielding from scrutiny and from the possibility of exculpatory evidence coming forward if that list is not available to the public. So I think we have to balance the necessity of notifying people - and there's been a long time to be able to do that - versus the public trial and the public interest in testing the ICMP's results.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's leave the matter for some time and limit our discussion to this document which is in front of us. Because, Mr. Vanderpuye, you indicated it may be possible that -- to produce a public redacted version of this one. What would remain?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Only the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the ICMP comment will disappear as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, the association with the ICMP would disappear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In order to make a more informed decision, the Chamber would prefer to have written submissions from the parties. So we proceed, putting them under seal for the moment. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did we give the exhibit number for this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be Exhibit P4642, under seal. And it is my understanding, Mr. Vanderpuye, that you are going to produce a public redacted version of his -- Mr. Parsons's testimony in Popovic testimony. There are two versions, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You're right, Mr. President. You're right. I had offered for admission his prior testimony. P4636 should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And then we'll admit his public redacted version as Exhibit P4643.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I have just a couple of questions left for Mr. Parsons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Dr. Parsons, could you, if you know, can you tell us how many individuals appear in the ICMP match report list, the spreadsheet that I've just shown you, that are associated with the Srebrenica events, through -- current through August of 2011.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That list represents 6.530 different individuals. That are on the main Srebrenica list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when you say represents individuals, do you mean named individuals, or does this correspond to the number of individual DNA profiles?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: It corresponds to named individuals with the caveat that sometimes we can't distinguish, for example, between siblings. But those would be named individuals as opposed to unmatched DNA profiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you approximate or do you know how many unmatched DNA profiles relate to that particular exhibit through August of 2011?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: From graves identified to us by the ICTY as being related to the fall of Srebrenica, we, in addition to these identified individuals, have unique DNA profiles representing 166 additional people. We haven't been able to identify them, but we know that they are victims and we know that they are uniquely represented by their DNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the most current information you have available to you is as concerns the number of individuals that are associated with the Srebrenica event?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Just the day before yesterday, we forwarded to Defence and the Office of the Prosecutor an updated list of identical constitution to the one that we just described, and in that list we have now made some additional matches and that number is 6.606 individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Does that include uniquely identified DNA profiles or just named individuals?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That is exclusive of the unmatched unique profiles I mentioned earlier. So the total number of individuals whose fate is known through DNA would be the sum of those two, 166 plus 6.606, and if my math is correct, that is 6.772 individuals known by DNA as associated with those graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: One last question, Dr. Parsons. Could you tell the Trial Chamber if the ICMP is charged with or responsible for notifying family members as to the disposition of their relatives?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No. The ICMP does not notify family members. That the job of the court-appointed pathologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Parsons. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Shall we deal with associated exhibits. First, I'd like to hear whether there is any objection from the Defence first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 65 ter 4119, I take it this is his expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: 411 -- I'm sorry, Mr. President, bear with me one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Methodology report 2001 to 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Then it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We would rather admit it as his expert report, not as part of associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 65 ter numbers 21043 and 21191. I think those two files were dealt with during the course of cross-examination in the Popovic case, but I wonder there are English translation for those reports. Further, in case of 21043, I can say it forms an indispensable and inseparable part of the transcript, but with respect to the other, i.e., 21191, I'm not sure if it forms an inseparable and indispensable part because Dr. Parsons merely confirmed what that document is about and offered no other comment. So in order to admit that document, probably you need to go through the document or leave it to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will leave that to the Defence. I don't think that it is material to a fair understanding of his prior testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But about the English translation of 21043.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have to apologise. I don't know what the status of that is. I will have to check it at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will mark for identification for the time being. And we'll not admit 21191 as part of associated exhibits. And lastly, 23659 seems to be a bit different one from that was dealt in the Popovic. Because in the Popovic document, it is described as an 80-page document but now it is 120 pages long. So could you deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, I can explain that. In the Popovic -- and I think it's just an error. In the Popovic transcript it dealt with the same individual but it dealt with a case file relating to a different match of a different body part. In this particular instance, I think 23659 deals with the matching of a body part of a sample -- the predominant sample of which was a tooth. And I think in the Popovic case it was just -- it was another part of the individual. But in either event, I have not used it with this witness. I don't know that it is material to the Popovic testimony either, except for he identified a couple of pages in it, which I think the Trial Chamber can reasonably glean from the transcript. So I don't think that needs to come in either. As it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you're not tendering it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's fine. We'll not admit it then. And we didn't deal with it -- by saying you have no objection, you would not object either to the addition of several documents to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then that's it. With the exception of those two documents, everything will be admitted and be given numbers in due course. While we're marking for identification, pending English translation with respect to 65 ter 21043. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, before the cross-examination begins, I'm wondering if I can just ask the Prosecution for clarity whether or not it's the Prosecution's case that this total number that's given by Dr. Parsons today, 6.530, are the number of victims of crimes for which Dr. Karadzic is being held accountable or whether they represent a number of people including those who died in combat in the Srebrenica events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to respond, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Robinson. It is the Prosecution's position that the victims that are indicated in this list are the victims of the crimes, mass executions, that are charged in relation to the Srebrenica events. You may hear other evidence in this case that explains a few of those victims, but I would say that our position is that, for the most part, the vast majority of those individuals, they are victims of executions as charged in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Parsons. I hope that you can hear me and I think perhaps it would be good if you, yourself, come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I can hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After you worked at the Smithsonian museum, you were employed -- or you got a job in the US military; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I was a contractor for the United States Armed Forces DNA Identification Laboratory, not a member of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you were working on the same kind of work, DNA identification; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many years did you work in the military?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I was associated with the AFDIL, A-F-D-I-L is the acronym, laboratory for 14 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you have any connections with that lab when you were working at the Smithsonian and what exactly was your job in the Smithsonian?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I did not have connections with the AFDIL laboratory when I was at the Smithsonian. At the Smithsonian Institution, I was a DNA scientist studying evolutionary biology and population genetics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And as for those 14 years, you had a contract with the military. You were employed there and you worked in that lab; right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, during that period of time, were you asked to come and testify before a court of law as an expert?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then you moved to ICMP; right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Throughout that period, before you came to the ICMP, were you an expert before a court of law?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like us to go back to Srebrenica. When did you exactly transfer to the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The year was 2006. I believe the month was March.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you received some basic information there. Did you receive any information in terms of the number of different locations that are involved in the events in Srebrenica that were investigated by the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So how many locations were involved?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I don't recall precisely, but it depends also on what you refer to as an investigation. ICMP has been involved in many reconnaissance efforts to investigate the potential for mass graves or other remains recoveries. We have attended thousands of sites throughout the former Yugoslavia in the course of our work. And the number of large mass graves associated with Srebrenica that we have investigated over the course of time has been 91.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about ICMP and all of Bosnia-Herzegovina? How many mass graves were investigated throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: We've responded to over 3.000 separate investigations, representing hundreds of mass graves. I don't have a precise value. And, again, it depends upon your definition anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you define this for us: The graves that you investigated, were they mass graves only, invariably?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No. We have any number of types of contexts from which we recover human remains. They could be single graves. They could be surface remains. They could be remains that are found in wells or natural depressions, river courses, any number of different environmental contexts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me try now to respond to your request to define investigations. Is it correct that ICMP deals with anthropological and anatomical investigations after excavations and exhumations, then DNA, DNA profiling, and identification, as a whole? Identifying the witness -- the victims, that is.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes to everything you said except for the fact that the ICMP does not -- is not competent to make legal identifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you explain that? Who does that? And what is the role in -- of the ICMP in all of that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The ICMP assists the government in Bosnia with the forensic analysis but it is the job of court-appointed forensic pathologists, officials of the Bosnian government, to issue death certificates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Uh-huh. I see. Is my understanding correct, that the pathologists that you engage, you, as the ICMP, do not necessarily have to be those that will assist with legal identification, that will take part in legal identification?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: All the pathologists that we work with are the court-appointed pathologists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is incorrect that -- out of all the things that I said? The pathologists that are court-appointed, were they appointed for participation in the work of the ICMP? Were these pathologists given to you in the process of legal identification?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No, sir, because the process of legal identification is not our remit. We provide forensic assistance to those pathologists who are in that official capacity. So the simple answer is that those pathologists are not part of the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the first part -- and I assumed that you confirmed that the ICMP deals with anthropology and analysis, that kind of investigation. Who does that for you, in addition to archaeologists? Is this also done by pathologists?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: In addition to forensic archaeologists, the ICMP has maintained a variable sized number of staff that are expert in anthropological examination and so we do have world-class subject matter expertise representing both the fields of forensic archeology and forensic anthropology who work directly for us and also assist the pathologists and work under the authority of the pathologists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who is the ICMP answerable to?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The ICMP is an international organisation originally established in 1996 as -- at a G-7 conference in Lyon, France, as a multinational initiative largely put forward initially by President Bill Clinton, then-president of the United States. The commission itself represents a chairman of the commission that is appointed by traditionally the US Department of State, but then maintains a number of additional commissioners who represent the governing body of the ICMP and these are diplomats and politicians and that type of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah-ha. So who is it that supervises the work of the ICMP? The State Department?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No, not the State Department. It's the commission itself that is the mantle under which ICMP works. So it's the board of commissioners, which, in fact, has international representation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah-ha. So how is the ICMP financed?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: We have funding from a wide range of governmental donors and a very, very small number of private foundations. The latter contribute very, very small amount, but typically it is governments who are interested in the progress of peace and reconciliation in Bosnia who fund our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah-ha. All right. Let us now look at this. Which governments are these?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The list total over time I believe exceeds 20 different governments. And, I'm sorry, but I won't be able to give you a comprehensive list. By memory, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we expect to receive this list by tomorrow? Because we shall certainly be continuing tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I don't see any impediment to my receiving that information prior to tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From a professional point of view, is there a scientific authority that checks the work of the ICMP? From a professional point of view, who is the ICMP answerable to?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, first and foremost, is the international accreditation process that was described in earlier testimony by which we are -- are inspected with great rigor by technical specialists as well as quality management specialists, who review all aspects of our SOPs and in addition review the conduct of our scientists in the course of performing their actions in comparison to those written SOPs. There are many other components that -- that give rise to the validity of ICMP's results by virtue of expert exposure. One of those is our steering committee on forensic sciences and this is something that has been empanelled at the ICMP for many years. In fact, I was originally on that panel before I joined the ICMP as its forensic science director. And this is a group of approximately 12, sometimes it -- it varies around that number, world famous forensic science experts who are given full exposure to ICMP's methods, assist us with evaluating our policy, work with our staff to understand what we do, how we do it, and the -- the -- immense challenges that we face. And the primary purpose of this forensic sciences steering committee, which meeting at least annually, is to make sure that we are staying abreast of developments in the scientific field and that we are bringing the best science that we can to bear on these issues. We have also engaged in a number of testing situations where the work that we have done has been duplicated by other laboratories, and to -- to achieve concordant results.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Excellent. You brought me to my next question. Your samples, are they checked somewhere else, according to the double-lined method, and, if so, where, and on the basis of which methods?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The samples in the former Yugoslavia that are the subject of this proceedings are not duplicated -- duplicate tested elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about this committee? Is that a private association or is it somebody's property? The committee that supervises you professionally.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No, it is not incorporated in and of itself outside of the fact that these are experts, renowned experts in the field that have agreed to assist the ICMP by serving on an advisory committee. This is a very common type of thing with organisations or efforts facing uniquely complex or difficult processes. In the World Trade Centre identifications being performed in New York City, they empanelled a series of scientific advisors very similar to the one that I'm describing at the ICMP. In fact, I served on that World Trade Centre advisory panel as well. The Armed Forces DNA Identification Laboratory for the United States also has a science advisory board made up of basically volunteer premier scientists who make themselves available to assist in that manner. So it's a model that is widely used and is extremely beneficial to the efforts that are involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I have to go back to this again. Who is the ICMP answerable to? Or is it sovereign?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I don't have an answer that would expand on the answer that I previously gave you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was in charge of verifications and possible investigations of possible misconduct or abuse committed by the ICMP or its departments?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: There is no agency that investigates misconduct or abuse by the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: However, I will hasten to add that a critical component of accreditation relates to the veracity of our results and the quality by which the laboratory operates and the standards of its staff. Our quality management system, which you have a copy of, contains a great deal of detail relating to the steps that we take to guarantee the extremely high quality of our results to include ethical standards of the staff to which they are trained and held accountable internally, as is the case in virtually all such organisations, as to again the ethical conduct and proper operation of this forensic accredited laboratory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If somebody objected to your work, who could they report you to? Who could initiate a procedure?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, they could certainly come directly to us and we would feel -- depending on the merit of the inquiry respond appropriately. Transparency and accountability is extremely important to us, to the ICMP, and throughout our existence we have gone to great measures to try to answer such questions exactly as that. And that's the basis of the scientific advisory board. We frequently bring scientists in to go through our laboratories. We are very open about our methodology and we are considered globally as essentially the world's leader in this type of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Or, to be more specific, there is no way of checking your work. Partners have to trust you; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, that is not right. That doesn't flow from the witness said. He said, in fact, if you analyse it, quite the opposite.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But may I ask the witness: How come we report them to them? If there was any abuse, we report them to them. Are they going to say that we are right? Are they going to investigate? Are they going to say that we are right? Are they going to say that they had not worked properly or that there had been abuse on their part?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I don't think asking me questions is going to elicit the answer that you want. It might be a useful idea to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I asked you whether I could put this question to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So here goes. I'm putting the question now. Does that mean that I could not report any abuse to anyone but you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, you could report allegations to whoever you feel like reporting allegations to. Credible allegations would be taken quite seriously by the ICMP, up to and including the level of the commissioners. And in fact, we responded to questions and inquiries very, very often. There are also a myriad of swirling allegations that can be found anywhere on the internet about virtually anything associated with these crimes and the situation, and those we don't necessarily respond to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since the State Department appoints the chief director, what is the responsibility and influence of the State Department in the sense that I've been putting my questions in?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: State Department does not have any formal responsibility for the conduct of the ICMP. It is a substantial donor to the ICMP, and the fact that that support continues is representative, I believe, of their contention and belief that the work we do is extremely beneficial to the peace and reconciliation process in Bosnia and other parts of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did I understand this correctly: As for the use of your findings, it is very important to have a certificate? An authorised institution should provide you with a certificate?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, I described the fact that we are internationally accredited. I don't know what type of a certificate you're referring to. We have an accreditation certificate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who did you get it from and when?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The German national accreditation agency called the Deutsche Akkreditierungsstelle. And the DNA laboratory system was accredited in October of 2007 and the DNA matching component was accredited about nine months later. That's the identification co-ordination division.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So up until 2007, and nine months after that, so 2008, you worked without accreditation; right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That's correct. When I joined the ICMP in 2006, there was an increasing movement in forensic laboratories around the world to include criminalistic laboratories working for the police to seek international levels of accreditation. Actually, at that time, it was not particularly common for laboratories working in forensic DNA analysis to be accredited. And there was a study by the European Network of Forensic Science Institutes. This is an organisation of laboratories that work together and address issues like requirements for accreditation, et cetera. A survey was taken at the same time that the ICMP was evaluating whether to take the steps toward accreditation what the percentage of criminalistic laboratories in Europe were that were accredited to the ISO 17025 standard, and 70 per cent of the laboratories at that time that were practicing within the criminal justice system were not accredited to that standard. It was noted, however, that many of them were working toward that accreditation, and this is an evolution of the quality assurance standards typical of the field. And it was at that time that the ICMP determined that we would also seek accreditation. We didn't change how we did our work, but we took the steps required to put it under the mantle of a formally constituted quality management system and, moreover, to adhere very carefully to a set of documentation that exceeded what we had before. So primarily our work in becoming accredited related to - I'm sorry, I must slow down - related to making sure that all our procedures were very carefully documented and that the staff was -- the staff's training, apart from their pre-existing expertise, which was world class, that their training was documented in the standardised way, and that competency assessments that were -- are regularly put in place and monitored continuously. Now this was a very easy process for the ICMP and many laboratories seeking this level of accreditation will take years to do it, but, in fact, the ICMP was very well prepared to take those steps toward accreditation because our procedures were so robust and our staff was so well trained. So it was a very short period of time, actually, to -- to formally accredit both of the aspects of the DNA identification process. That does not mean that our work that was conducted previously would be invalid. In fact, it remained among the best work being performed in the world at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It seems to me that the interpreters would like us to speak slower so I shall try to do that and I kindly ask you to take that into account as well. So some international body or committee or whatever would be checking your methodology. Do you agree that when you appear as a court expert witness, the Defence has the right to see not only what your methodology is but also the results involved and the correctness of those results?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The ICMP considers that it is a reasonable request on the part of Defence to be able to examine representative case work by the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you obtain material yourselves or do you receive samples for testing from pathologists?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: We obtain our samples in a number of ways. In many instances, it is the latter that you just said, which is pathologists who are handling the case cut samples from the remains and submit them to us directly. In other instances, the ICMP has seconded staff members assisting directly in the mortuary facility that is under the court-appointed pathologist's control. In those instances, ICMP anthropologists will often perform the sampling and examination of the skeletal remains in accordance with the world-class subject matter expertise and those would be submitted to the ICMP. They are submitted under the authority of the court-appointed pathologist, but, in fact, the technical manipulations are conducted by ICMP anthropological staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do the pathologists receive any kind of return information; and, if so, in what form?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The official product of the ICMP DNA testing and matching operations are the DNA match reports which were the subject of previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are these reports coded?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: When submitted externally, yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the pathologist who sends the sample, does he receive return information in the form of a coded report or coded findings?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And is there any reason for proceeding in this way? Why is this coded?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Those reasons have already been addressed. Would you like me to repeat them?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not talking about publishing these. I am asking whether this Defence could receive uncoded profiles, pherograms, simply checkable profiles that are not confidential?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, you've changed subjects as near as I can tell. First, you were asking about pathologists and now you're asking about Defence. Could you clarify, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First you said that whenever going outside of the institution, it's coded. So you even code it to the pathologist who sent the sample in. So I'm asking the reasons for that. You said that you already talked about that. So now I'm asking you this: Does the Defence have the right to receive the materials in order to look at them without the material being coded?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The ICMP --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, doctor. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm not sure in what context Dr. Karadzic has put the question. If he is referring to the Defence's rights in terms of a legal obligation, then obviously this is not the appropriate witness to put it to. If he is referring to it in a more colloquial way, as in could the Defence obtain this material, then I think it would be an appropriate question. So I would just ask for a clarification as to in what context he means because he has made prior reference to when you come here to testify does the Defence have this right, and that is a purely legal question which I don't think Dr. Parsons in his expertise has the competence to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Without delving into that legal detail, can you answer the question, Dr. Parsons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I can give a helpful comment and that is that the ICMP, in the interests of transparency and a recognition of the desirability of the Defence to be able to examine primary scientific data, is willing to make available to Defence case files containing the raw and uncoded data in the event that family members have given their specific consent to release that information, and we are willing to take extraordinary steps to make that available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you have a database; is that correct? DNA database.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And is this database specifically for Bosnia and Herzegovina, unique to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and is it stratified in any way?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No, it is not unique to Bosnia-Herzegovina. We have come over the years on the basis of our success in identifications in Bosnia and other parts of the former Yugoslavia to have a more global mandate for our work. And our database is then constituted of a number of different projects from around the world relating either to mass fatalities in association with transportation incidences, natural disasters, or other instances of human rights violations from other contexts, such as South Africa or Chile. And indeed, the database is compartmentalised, if you will, with regard to those different projects.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And are you able to tell us, please, whom this broader mandate came from? Who give you this broader mandate?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: In 2003, we returned to the governments that were involved in establishing ICMP and presented them with the concept of an expanded mandate on a case-by-case basis as appropriate to engage in these other types of activities, and the agreement was forthcoming that under the oversight of the ICMP commissioners, that this would be an acceptable expansion of our mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And does that refer to the countries whose governments issued that agreement or does that apply to all the countries in the world?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No. The ICMP has not been authorised by any type of a vote or a resolution that encompasses all the countries of the world. When we do provide assistance to other governments, those are going to be based on agreements with that government as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you also apply to tenders or make offers in a commercial kind of situation whenever there are identification jobs required?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No. The ICMP does not consider itself to be a commercial DNA laboratory. So in general, we do not respond to tenders. An exception to -- what might look like an exception to that is transpiring right at the moment with regard to a request for proposals that have been put out by the United Nations in association with the identification efforts of human rights violations from Cyprus. And they put out a request for proposals, which includes information for how much it would cost if the ICMP or whatever responding agency would undertake that work. But -- and in fact we are providing that information. Also, when we work for -- when we work in support of Chile, we have provided them with information regarding how much it costs us to do a DNA test and that is among -- that something that they cover as a fee. But we are not a commercial entity in the market of DNA testing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, we'll stop here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll -- hearing is adjourned. And we'll resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 22nd day of March, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.
